Perspective taking / ToM + moral reasoning

Between 9 and 12, moral cognition shifts towards coordinated, principle-based reasoning that recruits third-person perspective taking (while remaining anchored in rule-following and appeals to authority). By 12, most children can simultaneously represent the perspectives of multiple actors (including a neutral observer) and use this coordination to adjudicate conflicts between motives, duties, and consequences (Selman’s "mutual/third-person" level that typically emerges across roughly 10-12+ years) 1, 2. This social-cognitive upgrade scaffolds several moral advances in this window, with "third-order" theory of mind supporting reasoning about nested beliefs and reputation management 3, and cognitive empathy showing rapid gains that make it easier to forecast how different parties will evaluate the same act 4. Applied to resource and fairness dilemmas, children around 10-11 often rectify group-level inequalities with no in-group bias and a tendency to allocate more to disadvantaged out-groups 5, and by the end of the window many endorse equity when effort or productivity differs (even if outcomes are unequal) while also becoming more capable of jointly weighing need and effort 6, 7. Their judgments also grow more permissive of necessary harms to prevent greater harms, reflecting increased tolerance for trade-offs and side-effects in complex scenarios 8. In Kohlberg’s framework, most children here sit in the conventional stage, prioritizing shared norms and perceived expectations (especially of authorities) when justifying moral choices, even as perspective-taking and principle-based reasoning begin to loosen a strict dependence on authority pronouncements 9.

Pragmatics

Pragmatics becomes adult-like in ways that nine-year-olds typically cannot yet sustain. By twelve, children reliably infer speaker intent in nonliteral language, distinguishing ironic compliments from sarcastic criticisms, tracking attitude and politeness goals, and using prosody and context to recover "what was really meant" 10; they can now modulate their interpretation of irony based on what the listener knows 11, meaning they model common ground and adjust their pragmatic readout accordingly (something far weaker before this age window). Relatedly, faux-pas detection (recognizing when someone unintentionally says something socially inappropriate) improves across late childhood; nine-year-olds succeed in simple stories, but by  11-12 performance is robust across subtler narratives, indicating more reliable access to second-order beliefs ("she didn’t know he didn’t know…") 12.

Self identity

These children also undergo a fundamental shift in how they conceptualize themselves, moving from concrete, role- and behavior-bound descriptions toward a more abstract, integrative identity that explains actions in terms of enduring motives, principles, and trade-offs. Their value descriptions become more abstract, more likely to transcend specific situations, and more motivation-based rather than behavior-based 13: a child who once said "I help my mom with dishes" now articulates "I care about being helpful to people." Across this same window, children develop the capacity to increasingly resolve value conflicts and take stances that reflect their value priorities, such as when the desire to "care for others" conflicts with the desire for status or power 14. This represents a shift from holding multiple, potentially contradictory self-concepts in separate mental compartments to actively integrating them into a coherent hierarchy. In parallel, they move beyond compartmentalizing different "selves" across home, school, and peer contexts, learning to compare and reconcile contrasting self-descriptions ("I’m outspoken with friends but cautious in class") into higher-order traits and conditional rules that preserve coherence across settings, rather than treating them as disconnected identity fragments 15. This integration process essentially builds a value-based operating system for identity, where abstract motivational states govern behavior across contexts rather than context-specific behavioral scripts.
